title: Lesson 26: Contracts and Scoping: Statements of Work, Boundaries, and Avoiding Scope Creep
description: What a statement of work is for, how to draw a scope boundary that protects both sides, and how to keep an evolving engagement from silently becoming an unbounded one.

questions.question: What is the actual job of a written scope or statement of work?
options: To satisfy a legal requirement and shift blame onto the client
To replace a fragile shared memory of a verbal agreement with something both sides can inspect
To lock the price so it can never change under any circumstances
To list the deliverables while leaving the exclusions unstated
questions.explanation: A written scope replaces an unreliable shared memory of the conversation with a record both sides can inspect, so neither can drift from the agreement quietly.

questions.question: Where does most scope creep actually originate?
options: A client acting in bad faith to obtain free work
A written change process that prices every new request
Ambiguity, since when the work is never defined no change can be shown to be outside it
A retainer that names its included work in specific terms
questions.explanation: Ambiguity is the root of most scope creep: when the work is never defined, every addition looks reasonable because there is no boundary to exceed.

questions.question: A client asks for a small addition that was never in the original boundary. How should the request be handled?
options: Route it through a change process: scope it, price it, and add it as a separately agreed piece
Absorb it silently so the client stays happy
Refuse it, since any new request breaks the contract
Fold it into the existing scope and bill the hours at the end
questions.explanation: New requests are handled through an explicit change process that scopes, prices, and agrees them as separate work, which keeps the original boundary from expanding without a decision.
